headings.text: 1. Install and trust the toolchain with mise
2. Bring up the cluster and the full stack
How the stack is structured (for orientation)

blocks.html:
This is the first thing a core developer does on the new Kubernetes stack (pvarki/opendefence-platform, alpha): stand up a local kind cluster running the full Deploy App stack, so you can later point your local core code at it. Unlike the legacy stack there is no miniwerk and no CFSSL here — trust is provided by cert-manager, trust-manager, and the opendefense-pki resources, and the whole lifecycle is driven by task. Everything below comes from the platform repo's README.md and taskfile.yaml.

Prerequisites

  • Docker (kind runs Kubernetes in Docker).
  • kind — Kubernetes in Docker.
  • kubectl — the Kubernetes CLI.
  • mise — tool version manager (recommended; it pins the exact tool versions for this repo).

The pinned tool versions live in mise.toml:

[tools]
helm = "3"
kind = "0.31"
kubectl = "1.36"
task = "3"
yq = "4.53.2"
zarf = "0.76.0"

1. Install and trust the toolchain with mise

Once mise itself is installed, let it install everything else this repo needs and trust the local config:

mise install   # install all pinned tools (helm, kind, kubectl, task, yq, zarf)
mise trust     # trust this repo's local mise configuration

After this, mise automatically selects the correct version of every tool whenever you enter the project directory.

2. Bring up the cluster and the full stack

One command creates the kind cluster and deploys all resources:

task up        # create a kind cluster and deploy all resources
task down      # tear the cluster down
task           # list all available tasks

Under the hood (taskfile.yaml), task up runs cluster:create (creates a kind cluster named opendefense-kind from kind-config.yaml), check-kubecontext, cluster:wait (waits for nodes to be Ready), then deploy:local. The deploy is phased with readiness gates — it applies infra-phase1, waits for the CloudNativePG, cert-manager, and external-secrets operators to roll out, applies infra-phase2, waits for trust-manager, then applies monitoring and finally opendefense. Do not bypass this ordering; the gates exist so dependent resources only apply once their operators are ready.

3. Verify the kubecontext

task guards against deploying into the wrong cluster. You can check manually:

kubectl config current-context
# should contain: opendefense-kind

If the context is wrong, task check-kubecontext will warn and prompt before continuing.

4. Verify the pods

The core API runs as deployment/opendefense-rmapi in namespace opendefense-system, listening on container port 8000:

kubectl get pods -n opendefense-system
kubectl rollout status deployment/opendefense-rmapi -n opendefense-system
kubectl logs -n opendefense-system deployment/opendefense-rmapi

Supporting pieces run as operators in their own namespaces — for example cnpg-system (CloudNativePG), cert-manager (cert-manager + trust-manager), and external-secrets-system. You can confirm the gated operators are healthy:

kubectl rollout status deployment cnpg-controller-manager -n cnpg-system
kubectl rollout status deployment cert-manager-webhook -n cert-manager
kubectl rollout status deployment trust-manager -n cert-manager

How the stack is structured (for orientation)

The repo converts the legacy compose stack into Kustomize: each component is split into base/ (environment-agnostic) and overlays/<env>/ (registries, hostnames, certificates, ingress). Components are composed in phases under k8s/main/local (and k8s/main/cloud). See agents.md for the full structural contract; for everyday work prefer the task commands over hand-running kubectl kustomize.

Cloud deployment (for reference)

To build and deploy a Zarf package to an external cluster:

task zarf:package:cloud
zarf package deploy <package>.tar.zst --set OPENDEFENSE_HOST=example.dev.pvarki.fi --confirm

That is a deployment concern rather than a core-dev inner loop; see the Operate book.

Tear down
task down      # deletes the kind cluster
